t: Aim and plan of the session
n: In this session we learn to analyse xanthine derivatives. Topic: analysis of xanthine derivatives in the extract, with quantitative analysis carried out by UV spectrophotometry. Aim: to study the toxicological significance and analytical methods of alkaloids with weakly basic properties that pass into the organic layer in an acidic medium. The plan consists of two parts. The first: the toxicological significance of the purine alkaloids, that is, caffeine, theobromine and theophylline. The second: the methods of their analysis.

Now the expected outcomes. Students master the conditions for detecting alkaloids, xanthine and indole derivatives, by qualitative reactions both in a pure and in an unknown solution. They perform the qualitative reactions for caffeine, theobromine and theophylline. Remember: when tested with precipitating reagents for alkaloids, caffeine forms a precipitate. This precipitate serves as the first, preliminary sign.

Let us consider what is needed for the work. Necessary items: test tubes, separating funnels, reagents and visual materials. The session takes place in a room equipped with special laboratory facilities. For the murexide reaction a porcelain dish and a water bath are needed. For microcrystalloscopy a microscope slide and a microscope are used. For UV spectrophotometry an analytical balance, a 100 ml volumetric flask and ethyl alcohol are required.

This is the session map. At the centre are the purine alkaloids, that is, xanthine derivatives: caffeine, theobromine and theophylline. Their toxicological significance and analytical methods are included in the plan. Qualitative reactions: precipitating reagents, murexide, microcrystalline reaction, Nessler's reagent, TLC and UV spectrum. Quantitative analysis is carried out by UV spectrophotometry. Important numbers: theobromine Rf = 0.47, theophylline Rf = 0.22. The maximum of theophylline in 0.1 M HCl is 270 nm, and the absorbance is from 0.2 to 1.0.

We pay attention to the transformation of xanthine derivatives in the body. Caffeine is quickly absorbed and broken down in the body, so only a very small part is excreted in the urine. Theobromine undergoes N-demethylation. As a result, 3-methyl-7-methylxanthine and 7-methyluric acid are formed, and they are excreted in the urine. Theophylline is excreted in the urine as 1,3-dimethyl-, 3-methyl- and 1-methylurea. That is, each of the three substances is distinguished by its own metabolites.

We consider the reactions of caffeine in one place. Caffeine gives a precipitate with precipitating reagents for alkaloids, and under the action of HgCl2 needle-shaped crystals form. The murexide reaction, the microcrystalline reaction with mercury bromide and the red-brown colour with Nessler's reagent are also used. Physicochemical data: in the UV spectrum caffeine gives a maximum at 273 nm in ethyl alcohol and at 272 nm in 0.1 M HCl. TLC system: ether–acetone–25% ammonia, in the ratio 40:20:1.

t: Theobromine and theophylline: map of reactions
n: Now the reactions of theobromine and theophylline. Theobromine gives the murexide reaction. With Nessler's reagent it gives a light brown colour, and with Dragendorff's reagent it forms dark reddish needle-shaped crystals. For theobromine the Rf in TLC is 0.47, and its solution in 0.1 M alkali gives a maximum at 273 nm. Characteristic signs of theophylline: reaction with diazotised sulphanilic acid, Rf = 0.22 in TLC and 270 nm in 0.1 M HCl.

We compare the three substances side by side. In Nessler's reagent, caffeine gives red-brown and theobromine light brown. In TLC, theobromine Rf = 0.47 and theophylline Rf = 0.22. UV maxima: caffeine 273 nm, measured in alcohol. Theobromine 273 nm, in 0.1 M alkali. Theophylline 270 nm, in 0.1 M HCl. As can be seen, the medium of measurement also differs for each substance, and this must be taken into account when recording the result.

We consider the reagents in one list. For caffeine: perhydrol or another oxidant, ammonia, 0.1 M hydrochloric acid, 5% mercury bromide and Nessler's reagent. For TLC the system is ether–acetone–25% NH4OH, in the ratio 40:20:1. As the developer, 0.1 M iodine solution, then 96° ethyl alcohol and 25% HCl, in the ratio 1:1. For theobromine, 10% HCl and Dragendorff's reagent are needed. For theophylline, diazotised sulphanilic acid is used.

Safety rules. The student brings rubber gloves, a wipe and a face mask for the laboratory work. The examination is carried out in rooms with ventilation and a fume cupboard. These rooms are closed and sealed after the work is finished. Objects from infected persons, that is, those with tuberculosis, hepatitis or AIDS, arrive in a special container and are marked in the documents.

General information about purine alkaloids. The alkaloids of the pyrimidine series include the purine alkaloids, which are widely used in medicine. They are found in tea, coffee and other plants, and caffeine has also been obtained synthetically. Chemical names: caffeine is 1,3,7-trimethylxanthine, theophylline is 1,3-dimethylxanthine, theobromine is 3,7-dimethylxanthine. The position of the methyl groups in the names distinguishes these three substances from one another.

t: Caffeine: properties and conditions of isolation
n: Properties of caffeine and conditions of isolation. Caffeine in base form is readily soluble in chloroform, alcohol and water, and sparingly soluble in ether. It is extracted with chloroform mainly under acidic and partly under alkaline conditions. In medicine, caffeine is used in base form and also as the benzoate and salicylate salts. Remember: the conditions of isolation are tied precisely to the acidic medium.

Toxicological significance of caffeine. Caffeine has a stimulant action on the central nervous system and also stimulates the respiratory and other centres. It reduces the action of narcotic and hypnotic preparations. It is quickly absorbed and broken down in the body, and only a very small part is excreted in the urine. In toxicity, caffeine is weaker than theophylline, but in comparison with theobromine it has a stronger toxic action. Hence the order is: theobromine, the stronger caffeine, the stronger still theophylline.

About theobromine. It is found in cocoa and tea leaf and has also been obtained synthetically. On oxidation it breaks down into methylurea and methylalloxan. It hardly passes into the organic layer from a caustic alkali solution, whereas from an acidic solution it passes well. It stimulates cardiac activity and increases diuresis, and stimulates the central nervous system more weakly than caffeine. In the body it is converted into 3-methyl-7-methylxanthine and 7-methyluric acid and is excreted in the urine.

About theophylline. Theophylline is obtained from tea leaf and synthetically. It passes from an acidic solution into the organic solvent layer and is an isomer of theobromine. In medicine it is used as a powder and tablets, for example euphylline, theophedrine, antastman. It is used as a diuretic, an anti-asthmatic and in ischaemic heart disease. It is excreted from the body in the urine as 1,3-dimethyl-, 3-methyl- and 1-methylurea.

We compare the conditions of isolation. Purine alkaloids pass from an acidic medium into the organic solvent layer; this is the main condition of the session. Caffeine is extracted mainly under acidic and partly under alkaline conditions. Theobromine passes well from an acidic solution but hardly passes from a caustic alkali solution. Theophylline also passes from an acidic solution. Therefore we begin the extraction from the acidic medium.

Features of purification. In re-extraction, substances with weakly basic properties are lost, among them purine derivatives, narcotine, promedol, antipyrine and amidopyrine. Substances that sublime on heating, that is, barbiturates, benzoic and salicylic acids and caffeine, are purified by dry distillation. In the acidic isolate, weakly basic alkaloids are tested: caffeine, theobromine, theophylline, papaverine, narcotine and strychnine.

The plan for analysing caffeine. Stages of alkaloid analysis: isolation, purification, precipitating and colour reagents, physicochemical methods, determination of the amount. Caffeine is detected from the chloroform isolate: with the murexide reaction, mercury bromide crystals and the Nessler reaction. In physicochemical testing, the TLC system is ether–acetone–NH4OH, UV 273 nm. The amount of caffeine is determined by UV spectrophotometry at 273 nm.

Detection with general precipitating reagents. Purine alkaloids give a precipitate with general precipitating reagents. Scheibler's, Sonnenschein's and Dragendorff's reagents, as well as picric and picrolonic acids, are considered sensitive reagents. The reactions should also be repeated with pure alkaloids and a conclusion drawn by comparing the results. This is for now a preliminary examination, not a final conclusion.

The procedure for the murexide reaction. First stage: 1 ml of chloroform solution is evaporated to dryness on a water bath in a porcelain dish. Second stage: 1 ml of perhydrol or another oxidant is added to the residue and it is again evaporated to dryness. Third stage: 1 drop of ammonia solution is dropped onto the residue. If caffeine is present, a dark red-violet colour forms.

The essence of the murexide reaction. The residue is treated with an oxidant, that is, bromine or chlorine water, or nitric acid, evaporated to dryness, then ammonia is applied, and a red colour forms. Dimethyldialuric acid and dimethylalloxan combine to form tetramethylalloxantin. Theobromine and theophylline also give the murexide reaction. Therefore using only the murexide reaction does not lead to a correct result, since other alkaloids may also give it.

Microcrystalline reaction with mercury bromide. The residue on the slide is dried. To the residue, 1 drop of 0.1 M HCl and 1 drop of 5% mercury bromide are added. A certain time is allowed to pass. Then it is viewed under the microscope: if caffeine is present, needle-shaped colourless microcrystals are seen. The shape of the crystals should be drawn in the workbook.

Reaction with Nessler's reagent. If Nessler's reagent is added to a caffeine-containing isolate and heated, a red-brown colour forms. Theobromine gives a light brown colour with Nessler's reagent. The remaining reactions of theophylline are the same as the methods of detecting caffeine, according to this book. Thus, by the depth of colour, caffeine and theobromine can be distinguished.

Detecting theobromine with Dragendorff's reagent. To the dry residue on a microscope slide, 1 drop of 10% HCl and 1 drop of Dragendorff's reagent are added. Then it is kept for 10–15 minutes in a moist chamber and examined under the microscope. As a result, needle-shaped crystals of dark reddish colour and their clusters are found. These crystals indicate the presence of theobromine.

Distinguishing theophylline from theobromine. For this, the reaction with diazotised sulphanilic acid is used. Theophylline gives this reaction. Theobromine and caffeine do not give this reaction. An additional sign: theobromine dissolves well in CCl4, which distinguishes it from caffeine. Thus one reagent separates theophylline from the other two substances.

Thin-layer chromatography, that is, TLC. System: ether–acetone–25% NH4OH, in the ratio 40:20:1. The plate is sprayed with 0.1 M iodine, then with a mixture of 96° alcohol and 25% HCl, in the ratio 1:1. Bluish-pink spots then form. Rf values: theobromine 0.47, theophylline 0.22. We compare the position of the spots with these values.

Ultraviolet spectra. Caffeine absorbs light maximally at 273 nm in ethyl alcohol and at 272 nm in 0.1 M HCl. A solution of theophylline in 0.1 M HCl absorbs light maximally at 270 nm. A solution of theobromine in 0.1 M alkali absorbs light maximally at 273 nm. Remember: the value of the maximum also depends on the solvent, so when recording the spectrum the medium must be stated.

Preparing the standard solution for UV spectrophotometry. For the standard solution of caffeine, 0.1 g is weighed on an analytical balance and placed in a 100 ml volumetric flask. It is first dissolved in a small amount of ethyl alcohol, then made up to the mark with ethyl alcohol. The absorption spectrum of the solution is measured in the wavelength range 200–400 nm. The maximum is observed at 273 nm.

t: Measuring caffeine in the object by UV spectrophotometry
n: Measuring caffeine in the object by UV spectrophotometry. The absorbance of caffeine isolated from the object is measured at a wavelength of 273 nm. The reference solution is ethyl alcohol. Students record the spectra obtained in the workbook. The concentration of the solution is chosen so that the absorbance lies in the range from 0.2 to 1.0. In measuring the absorbance of a substance, a reference solution consisting of all the components of the solution under test is placed in the second cuvette.

Key numbers in UV spectrophotometry. For the standard solution, 0.1 g of caffeine is dissolved in ethyl alcohol in a 100 ml volumetric flask. The absorption spectrum is measured at 200–400 nm. The maximum of caffeine in alcohol is 273 nm. The concentration of the solution is chosen so that the absorbance is from 0.2 to 1.0. Ethyl alcohol is taken as the reference solution.

t: From the isolate to UV spectrophotometry
n: We consider the whole path from the isolate to UV spectrophotometry in sequence. Caffeine passes from the acidic medium into the organic solvent layer, that is, chloroform. For the murexide and microcrystalline reactions, the chloroform solution is evaporated and the qualitative reactions are carried out on the residue. The spectrum of caffeine is taken at 200–400 nm. The absorbance of caffeine isolated from the object is measured at 273 nm, and the reference solution is ethyl alcohol.

In the "T-table" task, concepts are given the correct definitions. For example, distinguishing theophylline from theobromine: diazotised sulphanilic acid. Solution of caffeine in ethyl alcohol: 273 nm. If caffeine is present, needle-shaped colourless crystals form; for this, 0.1 M HCl and 5% mercury bromide are used. Theobromine dissolves well in CCl4. Theophylline is used in medicine as a powder and tablets: euphylline, theophedrine, antastman. The substance that reduces narcotic action is caffeine.

Photometry methods. Determination of substances by light absorption is called photometry. It is divided into colorimetry, photocolorimetry and spectrophotometry. Colorimetry is determination of a coloured solution by simple visual comparison or with the help of a device. Photocolorimetry is measuring the substance in polychromatic radiation, in the visible part of the spectrum. Spectrophotometry is based on determination in monochromatic rays in the visible and also the adjoining UV and IR parts.

Requirements for choosing the wavelength. First, the sensitivity of the photocell receptors to the chosen wavelength must be high. Second, with a slight shift of wavelength the results must be close to one another. Third, the basic law of photometry must be obeyed. At the wavelength of maximum light absorption, the molar absorption coefficient is always large. Therefore measurement at the maximum is more accurate.

Interpreting the result and conclusion. In the analysis of alkaloids, 2 or more reactions and methods are used, without relying on the result of only one reaction. For purine alkaloids, using only the murexide reaction does not lead to a correct result. "Cadaveric alkaloids" formed in a putrefied object may also give some precipitation and colour reactions. The amount of the purine alkaloid detected is determined by the spectrophotometric method.

Group tasks. Group I: formulae of xanthine derivatives; toxicological and narcological significance of caffeine; why they pass from the acidic medium into the organic layer. Group II: forensic chemical significance of the general precipitating reagents and the murexide reaction; distinguishing the three substances. Group III: the amount of xanthine alkaloids; toxicological and narcological significance of theobromine and theophylline. Each group prepares its task and presents the result.

Review questions. First: write the formulae of the alkaloids containing xanthine, that is, a purine derivative; explain the toxicological and narcological significance of caffeine. Second: for what reason do xanthine derivatives more often pass into the organic solvent layer from an acidic medium? Third: what is the forensic chemical significance of the reactions of detection with general precipitating reagents and of the murexide-forming reaction? Fourth: how can caffeine, theobromine and theophylline be distinguished and separated from one another; how is their amount determined?

Conclusion and report. Caffeine gives a dark red-violet colour in the murexide reaction, needle-shaped crystals with mercury bromide, and a red-brown colour with Nessler's reagent. Theobromine forms needle-shaped crystals with Dragendorff's reagent, while theophylline is distinguished by the reaction with diazotised sulphanilic acid. UV maxima: caffeine 273 nm in alcohol, theophylline 270 nm in 0.1 M HCl. Absorbance is measured in the range 0.2–1.0.
